title: Let's Talk About COMBAT! (WITAWITADD)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y6T5kX1L0aw

Returning to the series after a long gap, Daniel (@dungeondive) takes on the genre's central verb and admits he rarely enjoys it. He's an experiential player who likes the broad strokes, and combat is where the nitty-gritty lives — usually a third or more of the runtime spent rolling for better numbers. The deeper problem is that it's static: tokens touch bases and dice happen, while the kinetic action he's picturing never appears on the table.

He sets two poles. At the bad end, an awakened Great Old One in Arkham Horror Second Edition or Eldritch Horror — twenty minutes of chasing fives and sixes that fizzles rather than climaxes. At the good end, Kingdom Death: Monster, S-tier, where combatants genuinely dance across the whole board and monster behaviour can be learned.

The rest is a taxonomy. Great combat in games he doesn't love: Myth ('the best game I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy'), Bloodborne, Gloomhaven, Mage Knight. Games he loves with dull combat: Shadows of Brimstone and Warhammer Quest 95 and their buckets of dice, Folklore, Mice and Mystics, most Games Workshop titles — with Dark Light Memento Mori improving on both parent and sibling via KDM-style spend-an-action dodges. Good combat he likes: Dungeon Universalis, Ghosts of Betwixt, Champions of Hara, Machina Arcana, Aeon's End, Hellboy. Most intense: Space Hulk, two verbs and a final standing roll. He closes on details worth stealing — initiative tracks from Folklore and Wander, Scarlet Heroes' fray die, Sleeping Gods' spatial damage grid.

----

Name a game you love whose combat you'd happily skip — and one whose combat is the whole reason you keep it on the shelf.
